speaker: Drago Anguelov
title: Inside Waymo's New Foundation Model Powering Self-Driving Cars [Drago Anguelov]
question: In fully autonomous driving, why do production teams often stop short of a single monolithic sensor-to-control model despite the appeal of end-to-end learning?
guest: End-to-end is a training strategy—passing gradients through the system—and it is orthogonal to whether you have modules in the stack. What we've learned over time is that you want a few large consolidated components so you can simplify development and scale them, rather than a bunch of little custom models. There is consensus that you need a few large components, but no consensus yet that it should be a single sensor-to-control component, and a lot of that comes from testability. If you go fully sensors-to-controls, you need a simulator that simulates over a million miles a day across over a dozen cameras, LiDAR, and radar realistically enough that it counts. Also, if you train one huge end-to-end model and need to fix something quickly, the only thing you can do is change the data and retrain—and you might break something else. In driver assist, it's less demanding, so you might get by with a fully end-to-end model. In fully autonomous driving, when you release it to drive millions of miles a week, you have to design your stack so you can validate it at scale and fix issues that arise.

points.core: End-to-end gradient training is orthogonal to having separate modules in a stack.
points.note: Accept: teams can consolidate into a few large components and still backpropagate across interfaces without collapsing to one black box. Do not credit: claiming end-to-end training and modular architectures are mutually exclusive.

points.core: Validating a monolithic sensor-to-control model requires ultra-realistic multi-sensor simulation at massive scale.
points.note: Accept: proving safety for an opaque sensor-to-control policy demands simulating huge mileage across cameras, LiDAR, and radar with high fidelity. Do not credit: generic statements that testing is hard without tying to sensor-level simulation.

points.core: Retraining a monolithic model to fix one issue risks breaking unrelated behaviors.

points.note: Accept: L4 autonomous fleets operating without a human fallback face a much higher validation bar than ADAS where end-to-end models are easier to ship. Do not credit: generic safety platitudes that do not contrast driverless autonomy with driver assist.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Production teams mostly stop short because a single black-box model is hard to verify, debug, and certify, not because it performs poorly on average.

When a monolithic network maps raw sensors straight to steering and braking, there are no inspectable intermediate outputs (detected objects, predicted trajectories, planned path), so a failure cannot be traced to a specific cause or fixed in a targeted way. A fix means retraining, which can silently regress behaviour elsewhere. That clashes with safety-case practice and standards such as ISO 26262 and SOTIF, which expect decomposable requirements, component-level testing, and evidence of behaviour in rare situations.

Data is the other problem: imitation-learned driving suffers from causal confusion and distribution shift, and demonstrating reliability across long-tail events purely by end-to-end testing would take impractical amounts of driving. Hard constraints such as traffic rules and collision-avoidance guarantees are also difficult to enforce inside a learned policy.

So the common compromise is "modular end-to-end": jointly trained but with interpretable interfaces for perception, prediction, and planning, often with a rule-based safety checker or fallback planner and redundant sensing paths around the learned core.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Production autonomous driving teams stop short of a single monolithic sensor-to-control network because safety-critical deployment requires hard guarantees, debuggability, and modular verification that pure black-box models cannot provide. While end-to-end networks excel at joint feature optimization in complex scenes, they offer no strict bounds against rare, catastrophic failures in long-tail edge cases. Production stacks therefore retain interpretable intermediate outputs—such as occupancy grids and planned trajectories—and pair learned policies with deterministic safety monitors and classical vehicle controllers. Decoupling trajectory planning from raw steering and braking lets physics-based controllers enforce kinematic limits, tire dynamics, and ride comfort, while allowing models to transfer across vehicle platforms and hardware calibrations without full retraining. Explicit interfaces also enable root-cause analysis and targeted fixes when on-road incidents occur, avoiding unpredictable regressions across the rest of the system. Finally, safety certification and regulatory cases depend on provable fallback maneuvers and component-level validation that an unconstrained monolithic network cannot guarantee.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Production teams usually keep some structure because they need to be able to verify, debug and certify the system, and a single opaque network makes all three hard. When a pixels-to-steering model makes a mistake, nobody can easily tell whether perception, prediction or planning caused it. That makes root-cause analysis, targeted fixes and regression testing much harder. Safety standards like ISO 26262 and SOTIF, along with regulators, expect requirements you can trace, parts you can test on their own, and evidence of behavior in rare edge cases. That's hard to show for a black box trained on imitation data.

The training signal is also a problem. Driving demonstrations contain almost no crashes or near-misses, so a policy trained only on the final driving output learns slowly. It can pick up shortcuts that don't reflect cause and effect, and it may handle long-tail situations badly.

So most teams build "modular end-to-end" systems instead. These are differentiable stacks trained jointly, but they still expose intermediate outputs like detections, occupancy, predicted trajectories and planned paths. Those outputs give extra supervision, let engineers look inside, and allow a rule-based safety layer or fallback controller to enforce hard limits. You keep most of the benefit of learning while still being able to test the system, swap out parts and meet safety requirements.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Production teams rarely deploy a single monolithic sensor-to-control network because safety-critical driving demands verification, debuggability, and deterministic guarantees that black-box models struggle to provide. When a monolithic system makes a dangerous decision, engineers cannot easily isolate whether the failure stemmed from perception, prediction, or planning, and retraining on new data to patch one edge case risks silently introducing regressions elsewhere. This opacity also complicates regulatory certification and incident audits, where teams must demonstrate why a vehicle acted as it did. Furthermore, traffic rules, kinematic limits, and collision-avoidance invariants are difficult to guarantee purely through learned weights, and capturing rare long-tail scenarios strictly from end-to-end demonstrations is extraordinarily data-hungry. Consequently, most production stacks adopt hybrid architectures—combining end-to-end learned components with interpretable intermediate representations like object tracks, occupancy grids, or candidate trajectories, all bounded by deterministic safety shields and fallback controllers that enforce hard physical and legal constraints.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
End-to-end learning is appealing because it can optimize for driving behavior directly and preserve information that hand-designed interfaces might discard. But a single sensor-to-control model makes it harder to diagnose why the car acted as it did, verify that it respects safety constraints, and predict what a retraining will change. Those problems matter most in rare, safety-critical situations, where training data is sparse and good average performance says little about the risk of a serious failure.

Production teams often use hybrid systems. Learned models may handle perception, prediction, and even trajectory planning, while explicit interfaces let engineers test components, replay failures, and isolate regressions. A separate safety layer can check proposed trajectories against vehicle limits and trigger a fallback. This keeps many of the benefits of end-to-end learning while giving teams concrete ways to validate and monitor the system.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
End-to-end learning can capture interactions that hand-designed modules miss. The production challenge is showing that the resulting vehicle behaves safely in rare situations. A model can perform well over millions of routine miles while relying on a visual cue that disappears in bad weather. If the car brakes too late, its steering and braking outputs alone reveal little about whether it failed to see a pedestrian, misjudged their motion, or chose an unsafe trajectory.

Many teams therefore keep interfaces they can inspect and test, such as predicted paths or a planned trajectory, even when they train several stages jointly. Those interfaces help engineers trace failures, test fixes against known scenarios, and check a proposed maneuver against physical limits before it reaches the actuators. This preserves much of the benefit of learning across the driving task while making it easier to build a safety case and maintain the system as it changes.
